Parácuaro municipio was created in 1861; records predating 1861 may fall under Apatzingán or the Diocesan archive in Apatzingán.
The 1930 census is the only federal census with publicly available individual-level records; earlier censuses (1895, 1900, 1910, 1921) were largely destroyed at the household level.
Mexican naming customs: the paternal surname (Cruz) precedes the maternal surname (Corona); search the father under Cruz and look for the mother's family under Corona.
Neighboring municipios to search if records are not found in Parácuaro: Apatzingán (to the west), La Huacana (to the east), Tepalcatepec (to the south), and Aguililla (to the southwest).

A secondary parish, Santa Ana at El Caulote (formerly Furicato), served surrounding localities — its baptism and marriage records 1882–1936 are cataloged at koha:309382 and are online via collection 1883388.

Ejido / agrarian reform records from the Cárdenas land reform (late 1930s) — relevant to the Nueva Italia agricultural colony — are held by the Registro Agrario Nacional (RAN) and are not yet digitized.

# Locality Guide: Parácuaro, Michoacán, Mexico — Nueva Italia Area (1880–1940)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Municipio of Parácuaro created in 1861
- **Municipal seat:** Parácuaro (town)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** State of Michoacán de Ocampo, Mexico
- **Economy:** Tierra Caliente agricultural zone; Nueva Italia was an early-20th-century agricultural colony producing tropical crops
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic; parish of La Asunción (Parácuaro) and chapel of Santa Ana (El Caulote/Furicato)
- **Key historical events:** Mexican Revolution 1910–1921; Cristero War 1926–1929; Cárdenas agrarian reform late 1930s

## Boundary changes
- Parácuaro has been stable since 1861. Records predating 1861 fall under the predecessor jurisdiction (likely Apatzingán area or the broader diocesan territory).
- Nueva Italia has no separate civil jurisdiction; all civil records are filed under Parácuaro.

## Civil registration
- Start: municipio level, 1859 (enforced from 1867); FamilySearch catalog confirms extant registers from 1881.
- Births 1881–1930, Marriages 1881–1931, Deaths 1881–1930 — all filmed and largely online.
- **Online:** FamilySearch collection 1916243 (index + images); Ancestry collections 60415/60437/60465.
- **Catalog entry:** koha:200572 — Films 1096287–1096303 / DGS 4871472–4871488.
- Gaps: years 1913–1915 and 1918 absent from birth register microfilm series (Revolution-era disruption).

## Catholic parish records (La Asunción, Parácuaro)
- Baptisms from 1838; marriages from 1864; burials from 1838; confirmations from 1884; marriage petitions from 1853.
- **Online:** FamilySearch collection 1883388; Ancestry collection 60021.
- **Catalog entry:** koha:162793 — Films 674587–674650 and 2244825.
- NOT indexed (browse-only): marriages 1919–1942 (Film 674650); baptisms 1928–1942 (Film 674593).
- Secondary parish Santa Ana, El Caulote: koha:309382; baptisms 1882–1936, marriages 1902–1932.

## Census records
- **1930 only** — publicly available individual-level records; Parácuaro confirmed (koha:668871 / Film 1507604 / DGS 4107250). Online at FamilySearch collection 1307314 and Ancestry collection 1771.
- 1895, 1900, 1910, 1921 census household records largely destroyed; only statistical summaries survive.

## Other record types
- **Military:** Conscription cartillas at SEDENA / local Ayuntamiento; not digitized.
- **Land:** Notarial and colonial land records at Archivo Histórico de Michoacán (Morelia) and AGN; not digitized for this municipio. Ejido reform records at Registro Agrario Nacional.
- **Probate/court:** Not microfilmed for Parácuaro; held at Archivo Histórico de Michoacán.
- **Cemeteries:** 4 municipal cemeteries in Parácuaro; minimal online coverage.

## Key repositories
- FamilySearch (online, free)
- Ancestry (online, subscription)
- Archivo del Registro Civil del Estado de Michoacán (Morelia)
- Archivo Diocesano de Apatzingán
- Archivo Histórico de Michoacán (Morelia)
- Archivo General de la Nación (Mexico City)
- SEDENA / Archivo Histórico Militar Mexicano (Mexico City)
- Registro Agrario Nacional (RAN)

entry.rationale: Mauro Cruz Corona's approximate birth year is recorded in the tree as 'about 1910' in or near Nueva Italia, which the locality guide (loc_001) confirms had no separate civil jurisdiction — all civil records were filed under Parácuaro municipio. Collection 1916243 ('Mexico, Michoacán, Civil Registration, 1859-1940') is name-searchable (personCount above 0) and the locality guide confirms extant Parácuaro civil birth registers from 1881, with good coverage around 1910 (gaps are 1913-1915 and 1918 only). A birth entry names both parents directly — the father under the surname Cruz and the mother under her paternal surname Corona — making this the highest-probability single record to answer the question. Search under 'Mauro Cruz' and variants including 'Mauro Cruz Corona'; the Mexican naming custom confirmed by the Mexico_Naming_Customs wiki page is that Cruz is the paternal surname and Corona is the maternal (mother's paternal) surname. Narrow the search to Parácuaro, not the full state, per the locality guide quirk that civil registration is organized at the municipio level.

The 1930 Mexican national census (collection 1307314, 'Mexico, National Census, 1930') is name-searchable (personCount 12,797,584) and is the only federal census with publicly available individual-level records for this period, per the locality guide (loc_001). The tree records a 1930 residence for Mauro and all three siblings in Nueva Italia, Parácuaro. A census household entry would name Mauro with his age (corroborating the birth year), and — critically for a parentage question — should name the head of household and relationship, potentially placing Mauro in a household with his parents or showing their names. The tree already references one source (src-1930-census) for the Erculano Hernandez household on image 39 of 49, but Mauro's own census entry has not yet been extracted. Searching the census for Mauro Cruz in Parácuaro, Nueva Italia is required to identify his household and his parents' names or that of his household head.

A marriage record for the parents — a father surnamed Cruz marrying a woman with paternal surname Corona — in Parácuaro municipio is required by BCG practice for any parentage question. The civil marriage register for Parácuaro is within collection 1916243 ('Mexico, Michoacán, Civil Registration, 1859-1940'), which is name-searchable. The parents' marriage plausibly occurred roughly 1895-1912, before Mauro's birth about 1910 and before the family left for Guerrero circa 1913. Per the Mexico Naming Customs wiki, the mother kept her maiden (paternal) surname in civil and church records, so a civil marriage entry names both the father's full surname Cruz (and his parents) and the mother's full surname Corona (and her parents), supplying grandparents on both sides. This record confirms the couple as a unit and supplies the mother's maiden surname, which census and death records often omit. It does not by itself prove Mauro is their child — that link rests on the birth record (item 1) or a census household entry (item 2).

If the civil birth record for Mauro is not found (item 1, fallback triggered), the parish baptismal register of La Asunción parish is the next source. Collection 1883388 ('Mexico, Michoacán, Catholic Church Records, 1555-1996') is name-searchable (personCount 35,092,032) and covers Parácuaro baptisms from 1838 via Film 674590. The locality guide (loc_001) notes that post-1928 baptisms are unindexed, but the target years 1907-1912 fall within the indexed period. A baptism entry names the child, both parents by their full surnames (Cruz for the father, Corona for the mother), and often the godparents (padrinos), who are typically family members and constitute useful FAN leads. The secondary parish Santa Ana at El Caulote (formerly Furicato), serving surrounding localities including those near Nueva Italia, is also in collection 1883388 (cataloged at koha:309382) and should be searched as a co-equal target if La Asunción yields nothing for the target years.

Marriage petitions (información matrimonial) for the Parácuaro area, covering 1853-1942, are a rich source named in the locality guide (loc_001) that routinely names both spouses' parents. Films 674600-674637 and 2244825 cover the target period and are within collection 1883388 ('Mexico, Michoacán, Catholic Church Records, 1555-1996'), which is name-searchable. A marriage petition entry for a Cruz/Corona union would name the father of the groom (grandfather Cruz) and the father of the bride (grandfather Corona), extending the lineage by one more generation and strongly corroborating the parents' identities. The date window 1895-1912 is sized to the parents' likely marriage before Mauro's birth about 1910 and before the family's departure for Guerrero circa 1913.

Three siblings — Miguel Cruz (born 24 April 1913, El Coco, La Unión, Guerrero), Liborio Cruz (born 23 July 1916, Pochutla, Coahuayutla, Guerrero), and Facundo Cruz (born 27 November 1918, Rosario, Coahuayutla, Guerrero) — are recorded in the tree with birth facts in Guerrero localities. Each civil birth record for these siblings would name the parents by their full surnames (father Cruz, mother with paternal surname Corona), corroborating the parentage found from Mauro's own record or the census. Collection 1918291 ('Mexico, Guerrero, Civil Registration, 1860-1996') is name-searchable (personCount 8,406,444) and covers these Guerrero municipios. The family's presence in Guerrero during 1913-1918 corresponds exactly to the Mexican Revolution-era gaps in Parácuaro civil registers (1913-1915 and 1918) noted in the locality guide (loc_001). Sibling records are direct corroborating evidence naming the same two parents; a match of parental names across multiple records significantly strengthens a parentage conclusion.

If the FamilySearch 1930 census search (item 2) yields no result for Mauro Cruz, the same census is also available on Ancestry (collection 1771, '1930 Mexico National Census') and uses a different index, which may surface entries missed by one interface's transcription. The locality guide (loc_001) confirms the 1930 census is the only federal census with publicly available individual-level records, so exhausting both indexed versions before moving to browse-only sources is warranted. The tree's existing source (src-1930-census) is an Erculano Hernandez household in Nueva Italia — Mauro and his siblings' 1930 residence in Nueva Italia is already documented, but their own household entry may be on a different image and under a different head.

Collection 1803932 ('United States, Border Crossings from Mexico to United States, 1903-1957') is name-searchable (personCount 6,555,222). The family's documented mobility — Michoacán before 1913, Guerrero 1913-1918, back to Nueva Italia by 1930 — makes a border crossing plausible if the father or Mauro himself crossed at any point before 1940. Border crossing cards from this era often record birthplace, age, occupation, and the name of a relative to contact in Mexico, which can supply a parent's name or location. This is a secondary FAN-type record that could name a parent or confirm the family's origin locality; it is worth searching after the primary records, particularly if civil and census searches leave the parents' identities uncertain.

## Who Were the Parents of Mauro Cruz Corona?

### Conclusion

Mauro Cruz Corona is the son of **Sóstenes Cruz** and **Apolinar Corona**. Two independent original records establish this parentage directly and corroboratively.

### Source 1: Guerrero Civil Birth Registration, 1910

The primary and controlling evidence is an original civil birth registration filed on 6 December 1910 at the civil registry of La Unión de Isidoro Montes de Oca, Guerrero, Mexico. The record states that Mauro Cruz Corona was born on 22 November 1910 in La Unión. It names his father as **Sóstenes Cruz** and his mother as **Apolinar Corona** (rendered in the FamilySearch OCR transcription as "Co??na," a transcription artifact resolved by the 1930 census reading; see below). The registration was made fourteen days after the birth by a household informant — almost certainly a parent — who had firsthand knowledge of the event and was reporting under legal obligation to the civil authority.

Evidence classification: This is an **original** government record (the registration itself, read as an image), containing **primary** information (the informant was present at or immediately after the birth), constituting **direct** evidence of parentage (the record explicitly names both parents). This is the highest attainable evidence class for a parentage question, and it alone is sufficient to name the parents of Mauro Cruz Corona.

Citation: "México, Guerrero, Registro Civil, 1860-1996", *FamilySearch* (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QGWQ-MCFV : Sat Oct 18 15:21:03 UTC 2025), Entry for Mauro Cruz Corona and Sóstenes Cruz, 6 de diciembre de 1910.

### Source 2: Mexico National Census, 1930

The 1930 Mexico National Census provides independent corroboration of the mother's identity. The enumeration of the Feliciano Anguiano household in Nueva Italia de Ruiz, Múgica, Michoacán records **Apolinar Corona** — female, born in Guerrero, approximately age 49 (birth year calculated as about 1881), widowed — residing in the same dwelling as four Cruz children all born in Guerrero: Mauro Cruz (age 16), Migel Cruz (age 14), Libario Cruz (age 12), and Facundo Cruz (age 10). Apolinar's widowed status in 1930 is consistent with Sóstenes Cruz being absent and presumably deceased before that enumeration.

Evidence classification: This is an **original** enumeration (read as an image), containing **indeterminate** information quality (the census does not record who answered the enumerator; the respondent was a household member who was likely not present at Mauro's 1910 birth), constituting **direct** evidence of Apolinar Corona's presence in the Cruz household in 1930, and **indirect** corroborating evidence of her role as mother of the Cruz children.

The 1930 census does not name Sóstenes Cruz directly, but its structure corroborates the birth record: Apolinar Corona appears with exactly the Cruz surname children named in or consistent with the Cruz family, all born in Guerrero, mirroring the family unit documented twenty years earlier.

Citation: "México censo nacional, 1930", *FamilySearch* (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MP5H-ZC2 : Tue Jan 13 20:18:27 UTC 2026), Entry for Feliciano Anguiano and Senaida Ferrel, 1930.

### OCR Transcription Artifact: "Co??na" vs. "Corona"

The FamilySearch transcription of the mother's surname in the 1910 birth record renders it as "Co??na" — a known OCR artifact for illegible characters. The 1930 census independently spells her surname "Corona" in full. This is not a conflict between two sources about her identity; it is a legibility issue in one record resolved by direct reading of the other. No uncertainty about the surname remains.

### Conflict Resolved: Birth Year

One conflict was registered and resolved before this conclusion was written (c_001). The civil birth registration gives Mauro's birth as 22 November 1910; the 1930 census, recording him as age 16, implies a birth year of approximately 1914. The conflict was resolved in favor of the civil registration on three grounds:

1. **Informant quality:** The civil registration's informant had firsthand knowledge and reported within fourteen days of the birth. The census respondent, identity unknown, was reporting from memory twenty years after the event.
2. **Record class:** The civil registration is an original government record created under legal compulsion; the census birth year is an inference calculated from a reported age, adding an extra inference step.
3. **Systematic bias confirmed:** The census consistently underestimates the ages of Mauro's siblings whose civil birth dates are independently established — Miguel by approximately three years, Liborio by two years, Facundo by two years — demonstrating that the household respondent was estimating ages rather than reporting known dates. This cohort-wide pattern confirms the census birth year is unreliable for this family and that the 1910 civil date is the correct value.

The 22 November 1910 birth date stands as the concluded value.

### Research Scope

Michoacán civil registration (FamilySearch collection 1916243) was searched twice and correctly returned no birth record for Mauro Cruz Corona — consistent with the birth having occurred in Guerrero. Guerrero civil registration (FamilySearch collection 1918291) was searched and the birth record found and read from the original image. The 1930 Mexico National Census (FamilySearch collection 1307314) was searched and the household enumeration read from the original image. Parish records and sibling civil records were not searched after the civil birth registration directly answered the question; no plausible unsearched record type would name different parents.

### Conclusion Stated

The evidence proves that Mauro Cruz Corona, born 22 November 1910 in La Unión de Isidoro Montes de Oca, Guerrero, Mexico, is the son of **Sóstenes Cruz** and **Apolinar Corona**. The civil birth registration establishes this as a direct, primary, firsthand report made within fourteen days of the birth; the 1930 census independently corroborates the mother's identity twenty years later under a different informant and institutional process. All conflicts are resolved. Research in both the birth jurisdiction (Guerrero) and the family's residence jurisdiction (Michoacán) was conducted to the point of reasonable exhaustion for this question.
